prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of Romanian prose, grounded in a lyric poetic imagination, in which memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation are built into a vast, densely patterned and singular imaginative architecture.

statement.case_for: My preferred laureate is unchanged, but I have narrowed the citation. The test I apply is whether there is a voice in this writer's work that I find nowhere else. On public knowledge of the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid, Cărtărescu meets it. Memory, the body, dream and cosmological speculation are joined in one recursive, highly patterned prose, and the project is sustained at large scale over decades. The chair asked which book I would test the depth-versus-repetition question against. I would use Solenoid set against the Blinding trilogy: does the later book rework the earlier materials into a different structure and a different pressure, or only restage them? From public descriptions it appears to do the former. I cannot verify that from the Romanian text, so it remains a judgment to be tested. The case is about voice, form and sustained imaginative depth under the common criteria and Nobel's will. It does not depend on nationality, political symbolism or the fact that every opening ballot named him first, and that convergence is not literary evidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my choice is that I may be rewarding scale. The recursion of motifs across very long books may be a closed circuit rather than accumulation. The achievement lives in dense Romanian wordplay, rhythm and syntax that the committee reads largely through translation, and my own profile records that I regret not being able to read some candidates in the original. If a reader of the Romanian showed that the patterning thins or the control slackens in the later large books, I would have to reconsider. The best rival cases are Michon, whose voice is recognizable within a sentence and who has the strongest claim on concentration of form, and Murnane, whose rigor is real and whose English can be judged without a translation gap. Neither displaces Cărtărescu for me. Their cases give weaker evidence of range and development across a body of work, but that weighting is a judgment, not a settled fact.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the whole-oeuvre claim is less well evidenced for the poetry and early work than for the major novels. He would ground the citation mainly in the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, with the poetry as a related strand, and he says the repetition question has to be answered from the books, not from reputation.
responses.response: This is the point that moved me. In round 1 I wrote that the poetry gives the prose its lyrical base and that the citation could cover the whole body of work. But I conceded that translated coverage of the poetry and early work is uneven, so that claim is only partly tested. I now think the citation is more honest if it names the prose as the evidenced core and treats the lyric imagination as its origin, not as a separately certified achievement. That is why my citation now reads as a body of Romanian prose grounded in a lyric poetic imagination. I also agree with Olsson that the repetition question is the real test. I have named Solenoid against the Blinding trilogy as my test case, but I have not read the Romanian and I do not claim to have resolved it.

responses.point: Palm argues that Cărtărescu's effect depends more on large-scale architecture and imagery, which she thinks survive translation better, than Michon's effect depends on syntax and cadence. On that basis she weighs Michon's translation loss as likely larger than Cărtărescu's.
responses.response: I agree with the direction of the argument, but I would hold it more loosely than Palm does. Structure, recurring imagery and large-scale design probably do travel better than cadence. Even so, the chair's question about whether the Romanian wordplay and rhythm survive cannot be answered by that distinction alone. If much of Cărtărescu's force is in the sentence, the translation risk is real for him too. It is also an inference about types of effect, not a verified comparison of translations. I would keep Michon as my first alternative and not claim the translation gap clearly favors Cărtărescu. A regional or Romanian-language expert assessment, as the chair suggested, would be the right evidence. I would not treat the argument as a substitute for one.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Murnane sixth and asks whether the narrowness of his method is discipline or a ceiling. She reads my earlier observation as supporting his durability but not his range, and she places Michon seventh because the compact corpus gives limited evidence of breadth.
responses.response: I accept her reading of what I said, and it is the reason Murnane is not my first choice. His late work extending the early method shows durability and a consistent voice, but not widening. On the criteria of sustained quality and significance across a body of work, range counts and a ceiling is a legitimate worry. I keep him as an alternative for a different reason. If the committee decides translation obscures too much of the Romanian, he is the shortlisted writer whose prose a committee can judge in the original English. That is a point about the quality of the evidence, not about merit. On Michon I would hold my round 1 position: the voice is strong, and I weigh that more favorably than Carlberg does, but not enough to move him above a larger, better-evidenced project.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that the major books reorganise the same materials at different scales and in different forms, which he reads as development. He also discloses long engagement with Central Europe as thematic proximity, and says he has tried to discount any familiarity effect.
responses.response: I made a similar argument in round 1, that motif recurrence is how the project accumulates meaning. After the exchange, I see that this is an assertion of reading, and it is the claim the chair asks us to test. Reorganizing the same materials at different scales can be development, but it can also be a polished repetition, and only the books can decide. I would ask that we separate the two by comparing specific structures, not by general description. On his disclosure, I note it and agree it is thematic proximity, not a tie. It is useful that he stated it. My own preference for historical and psychological fiction is also context, not evidence of preference.

uncertainties: How much of the patterning, wordplay and rhythm of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in the translations available to the committee. I have not independently verified any text and judge from public knowledge and translation.
Whether Solenoid and the other late large books deepen the project or restage earlier materials is untested against specific passages, and I am not claiming that it is settled.

Translated coverage of the poetry and early work is uneven, so any claim about a unified project across poetry and prose is only partly tested. This is why I now ground the citation mainly in the prose.
For Michon and Murnane, a compact or narrow corpus limits what can be said about range and development across the whole oeuvre.

I did not rank Carson, Zurita or Marilynne Robinson highly in my opening. Carlberg suggests that Carson's scope could centre on poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal, but I cannot yet assess whether the hybrid oeuvre could be fixed in a citation. How non-textual interventions would be treated for Zurita is also unresolved.
Carlberg's voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption and I do not rely on it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, and unchanged from round 1. My own work as a novelist and critic of historical and psychological fiction is context, not a documented tie to any shortlisted writer. I note Sem-Sandberg's disclosure of thematic proximity to Central Europe and treat it as context, not as a conflict. The full Swedish Academy decides the actual award and is not simulated.
